---
title: "Inheritance and abstract classes"
---

Two kinds of ball, two kinds of enemy, two kinds of invoice line. Programs are
full of things that are almost the same, and the quickest way to get the second
one is to copy the first class and change what differs. That works until you
have to fix a bug, and then you have to fix it twice. TypeScript has a better
answer, and it costs one keyword.

## Two classes, one number apart {#sec-inheritance-copy}

1. Create a new app from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. In `index.html`, replace everything between `<body>` and `</body>` with
   this:

   ```html
   <h1>Falling balls</h1>
   <svg id="stage" viewBox="0 0 300 300" width="300" height="300" role="img" aria-label="Two falling balls"></svg>
   <script src="./src/index.ts" type="module"></script>
   ```

3. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with this:

   ```ts
   const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';

   const stage = document.querySelector<SVGSVGElement>('#stage');
   if (!stage) {
     throw new Error('No element with the id stage');
   }

   class Ball {
     private y: number;
     private circle: SVGCircleElement;

     constructor(stage: SVGSVGElement, x: number, color: string) {
       this.y = 20;
       this.circle = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'circle');
       this.circle.setAttribute('cx', String(x));
       this.circle.setAttribute('cy', String(this.y));
       this.circle.setAttribute('r', '20');
       this.circle.setAttribute('fill', color);
       stage.append(this.circle);
     }

     fall(deltaSeconds: number): void {
       this.y += 100 * deltaSeconds;
       this.circle.setAttribute('cy', String(this.y));
     }
   }

   class HeavyBall {
     private y: number;
     private circle: SVGCircleElement;

     constructor(stage: SVGSVGElement, x: number, color: string) {
       this.y = 20;
       this.circle = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'circle');
       this.circle.setAttribute('cx', String(x));
       this.circle.setAttribute('cy', String(this.y));
       this.circle.setAttribute('r', '20');
       this.circle.setAttribute('fill', color);
       stage.append(this.circle);
     }

     fall(deltaSeconds: number): void {
       this.y += 300 * deltaSeconds;
       this.circle.setAttribute('cy', String(this.y));
     }
   }

   const light = new Ball(stage, 100, 'tomato');
   const heavy = new HeavyBall(stage, 200, 'slateblue');

   let lastTime = 0;

   const tick = (timestamp: number) => {
     if (lastTime === 0) {
       lastTime = timestamp;
     }
     const deltaSeconds = (timestamp - lastTime) / 1000;
     lastTime = timestamp;

     light.fall(deltaSeconds);
     heavy.fall(deltaSeconds);

     requestAnimationFrame(tick);
   };

   requestAnimationFrame(tick);
   ```

4. Run `npm start`.

Two circles drop from the top edge. The blue one is three times as fast, both
slide out at the bottom, and the SVG cuts them off there. Nothing catches them,
because these two classes know how to fall and nothing else.

Now read the two classes again. Forty lines, and exactly one number is
different: 100 in one `fall`, 300 in the other.

## One word deletes the copy {#sec-inheritance-extends}

Delete the whole `HeavyBall` class and put this in its place:

```ts
class HeavyBall extends Ball {
  fall(deltaSeconds: number): void {
    this.y += 300 * deltaSeconds;
    this.circle.setAttribute('cy', String(this.y));
  }
}
```

`extends Ball` says that a `HeavyBall` is a `Ball` with changes. It gets every
field and every method of `Ball` without repeating a line of them, including
the constructor, which is why `new HeavyBall(stage, 200, 'slateblue')` still
takes the same three arguments. `Ball` is the **base class** here and
`HeavyBall` is the **subclass**.

A subclass may replace a method it inherited by writing a method with the same
name. That is called **overriding**, and `fall` is overridden above.

VS Code puts a red line under the new class, and `npx tsc --noEmit` says why,
once for every place that touches a private member:

```
Property 'y' is private and only accessible within class 'Ball'.
Property 'circle' is private and only accessible within class 'Ball'.
Property 'y' is private and only accessible within class 'Ball'.
```

## What `protected` is for {#sec-inheritance-protected}

`private` shuts a field away from everything outside its class, and a subclass
counts as outside. That is the right setting most of the time, and it is
exactly wrong here, because `HeavyBall` has to reach the `y` it inherited.

`protected` is the middle setting: the class itself and every subclass can use
the field, and code outside the family cannot. Change the two field
declarations in `Ball`:

```ts
protected y: number;
protected circle: SVGCircleElement;
```

The errors disappear and the page animates again. Reach for `protected` when a
subclass needs the value, and leave everything else `private`, because a field
that subclasses may touch is a field you cannot rename in peace.

## A subclass constructor calls its base first {#sec-inheritance-super}

A subclass can bring its own constructor. Add a third kind of ball that fixes
its own color and size:

```ts
class BigBall extends Ball {
  constructor(stage: SVGSVGElement, x: number) {
    super(stage, x, 'gold');
    this.circle.setAttribute('r', '35');
  }
}
```

`super(...)` calls the constructor of the base class. Leave that line out and
TypeScript refuses the class, and the first error reads
`Constructors for derived classes must contain a 'super' call.`; move the line
below the `setAttribute` line instead and it says
`'super' must be called before accessing 'this' in the constructor of a derived class.`

Both messages guard the same thing. `this.circle` is created by the base
constructor, so until `super(...)` has run there is no circle to set an
attribute on. First let the base build its part of the object, then add yours.

Nobody creates a `BigBall` yet, so `npx tsc --noEmit` also reports
`'BigBall' is declared but never used.` The next section gives it a job.

## One array holds every kind {#sec-inheritance-array}

Three balls mean three variables and three calls in `tick`, and the fourth ball
would mean a fourth of each. Replace the `light` and `heavy` variables with one
array and let a loop do the work:

```ts
const balls: Ball[] = [new Ball(stage, 60, 'tomato'), new HeavyBall(stage, 150, 'slateblue'), new BigBall(stage, 240)];
```

Inside `tick`, replace the two `fall` calls with this:

```ts
for (const ball of balls) {
  ball.fall(deltaSeconds);
}
```

The array is typed `Ball[]`, and TypeScript accepts a `HeavyBall` and a
`BigBall` in it, because each of them is a `Ball`. One line calls `fall` on all
three, and every ball still falls at its own speed: the object knows which
`fall` belongs to it, and the loop never asks.

What the array type does control is which members you may use. Through a
`Ball[]` you can call what `Ball` declares. A method that only `BigBall` has is
not available in that loop.

## A class nobody should build {#sec-inheritance-abstract}

`Ball` now has two jobs, and they fight. It is the blueprint every kind shares,
and it is also a ball you can create, with a speed of 100 baked into `fall`.
Give the speed to the subclasses and the base class keeps only the part that
never changes. Replace everything from `class Ball` down to the `balls` array
with this:

```ts
const FLOOR = 260;

abstract class Ball {
  protected y: number;
  protected circle: SVGCircleElement;
  private landed: boolean;

  constructor(stage: SVGSVGElement, x: number, color: string) {
    this.y = 20;
    this.landed = false;
    this.circle = document.createElementNS(SVG_NS, 'circle');
    this.circle.setAttribute('cx', String(x));
    this.circle.setAttribute('cy', String(this.y));
    this.circle.setAttribute('r', '20');
    this.circle.setAttribute('fill', color);
    stage.append(this.circle);
  }

  abstract get speed(): number;

  protected abstract onReachedBottom(): void;

  fall(deltaSeconds: number): void {
    if (this.landed) {
      return;
    }

    this.y += this.speed * deltaSeconds;
    if (this.y >= FLOOR) {
      this.y = FLOOR;
      this.landed = true;
      this.onReachedBottom();
    }

    this.circle.setAttribute('cy', String(this.y));
  }
}

class LightBall extends Ball {
  get speed(): number {
    return 100;
  }

  protected onReachedBottom(): void {
    this.circle.setAttribute('fill', 'gold');
  }
}

class HeavyBall extends Ball {
  get speed(): number {
    return 300;
  }

  protected onReachedBottom(): void {
    this.circle.remove();
  }
}

const balls: Ball[] = [new LightBall(stage, 100, 'tomato'), new HeavyBall(stage, 200, 'slateblue')];
```

Both balls stop at the floor now. The red one turns gold when it lands, the
blue one disappears, and neither subclass contains a line about falling.

`abstract` marks a member that has no body here and must be filled in by every
subclass. `speed` is an abstract getter, so `this.speed` inside `fall` reads
whatever the subclass returns. `onReachedBottom` is an abstract method, and the
base class decides when it runs while the subclass decides what happens. A
class with an abstract member must be marked `abstract` itself, and such a
class cannot be created. Try `new Ball(stage, 50, 'green')` and TypeScript
answers `Cannot create an instance of an abstract class.`

Forget one of the two members in a subclass and the message names it. Delete
the `speed` getter from `HeavyBall` and TypeScript says:

```
Non-abstract class 'HeavyBall' does not implement inherited abstract member speed from class 'Ball'.
```

That is the whole point of an abstract member. It is a promise the compiler
collects, so `fall` can call `this.onReachedBottom()` and be sure something is
there.

Notice which fields kept which keyword. `landed` is `private`, because only
`fall` ever looks at it. `y` and `circle` are `protected`, because the
subclasses work with them.

::: {.callout-note}
## Still one file

All of this lives in `src/index.ts`, and the file grows with every kind of
ball. That is fine for now. The next chapter gives each class a file of its
own.
:::

::: {.research title="Gravity, and getting rid of dead balls"}
The bouncing balls below fall faster the longer they fall, the fragile ones get
paler with every landing, and the dead ones have to leave the array. This
chapter shows none of that.

1. A game loop keeps a speed in pixels per second and changes it every frame.
   Which two lines make gravity pull a ball down, one for the speed and one for
   the position, and in which unit do you give the gravity constant?
2. `filter` builds an array out of an array. What does the function you hand to
   `filter` have to return for an item to be kept, and what does `filter` do to
   the array you called it on?
3. SVG can make a shape see-through. Which attribute changes only the inside of
   a shape and leaves its outline alone, and which two numbers are the ends of
   that attribute's range?

Question 2 has to work without looking it up, because `filter` turns up in
every exam task that works with arrays.
:::

## Exercise: bouncing balls {#sec-inheritance-exercise}

Four kinds of ball share one base class and differ in two members.

{{< exercise bouncing-balls >}}

The `index.html` you copied holds an empty `<svg id="stage">` of 600 by 400 and
five buttons: `#addGummy`, `#addSteel`, `#addSuper`, `#addFragile`, and
`#clear`.

1. Create a new app from our template inside `coursework/`.
2. Replace everything in `src/index.ts` with `import './styles.css';`, the
   namespace constant `const SVG_NS = 'http://www.w3.org/2000/svg';`, and the
   numbers the simulation runs on:

   ```ts
   const STAGE_WIDTH = 600;
   const STAGE_HEIGHT = 400;
   const GRAVITY = 900;
   const MIN_BOUNCE_SPEED = 30;
   ```

   Run `npm start`. Expected result: an empty box with five buttons under it.
3. Look up the six elements with `querySelector<SVGSVGElement>` and
   `querySelector<HTMLButtonElement>`, and cover them with one `if` that
   throws.
4. Write `abstract class Ball` with these fields at the top: `protected y`,
   `protected velocityY`, and `protected radius`, all of type `number`, then
   `protected circle` of type `SVGCircleElement` and `private resting` of type
   `boolean`. The constructor takes
   `(stage: SVGSVGElement, x: number, radius: number, color: string)`,
   starts `y` at `radius` so the ball touches the top edge, sets `velocityY` to
   0 and `resting` to `false`, creates the circle with `createElementNS`, gives
   it `cx`, `cy`, `r`, and `fill`, and appends it to the stage.
5. Add the two abstract members. `abstract get bounciness(): number;` is the
   share of the speed a ball keeps when it bounces, so 0.5 means it comes back
   up half as fast as it went down. The method
   `protected abstract onReachedBottom(): boolean;` runs on every landing and
   returns `true` when the ball plays on and `false` when it is finished.
6. Add a method `remove()` that takes the circle out of the SVG.
7. Write `update(deltaSeconds: number): boolean`, the method the game loop
   calls once per frame for every ball. In this order:

   * when `this.resting` is `true`, return `true` and do nothing else;
   * let gravity change `velocityY` and let `velocityY` change `y`, the two
     lines from research question 1;
   * when `this.y` is greater than `STAGE_HEIGHT - this.radius`, the ball has
     reached the floor: pin `this.y` to that value and turn the speed around
     with `this.velocityY = -this.velocityY * this.bounciness;`
   * still inside that floor branch, when `Math.abs(this.velocityY)` is now
     below `MIN_BOUNCE_SPEED`, the ball has no bounce left in it: set
     `velocityY` to 0 and `resting` to `true`. Otherwise call
     `this.onReachedBottom()`, and when that returns `false`, call
     `this.remove()` and return `false`;
   * when `this.y` is smaller than `this.radius`, the ball hit the ceiling: pin
     `this.y` to `this.radius` and turn the speed around the same way;
   * write the new `cy` and return `true`.
8. Write `class GummyBall extends Ball`. Its constructor takes
   `(stage: SVGSVGElement, x: number)` and calls
   `super(stage, x, 22, 'hsl(0 80% 60%)')`. Give it a `private bounces: number`
   that starts at 0, a `bounciness` of 0.6, and an `onReachedBottom` that counts
   the landing, writes
   `` `hsl(${(this.bounces * 50) % 360} 80% 60%)` `` into `fill`, and returns
   `true`. In `hsl`, the first number is an angle on the color wheel, so a
   growing number walks the ball through the rainbow.
9. Write `class SteelBall extends Ball`: radius 16, color `'#8d99ae'`,
   `bounciness` 0.85, and an `onReachedBottom` whose whole body is
   `return true;`. Steel does not care that it landed, and an abstract member
   still has to be implemented.
10. Write `class SuperBall extends Ball`: radius 14, color `'#2ecc71'`,
    `bounciness` 0.9. Its `onReachedBottom` gives the ball an extra kick with
    `this.velocityY -= 150;`, grows `this.radius` by 2, writes the new radius
    into the `r` attribute, and returns `this.radius <= 40`, so the ball pops
    once it has grown too big.
11. Write `class FragileBall extends Ball`: radius 26, color `'#c4a77d'`,
    `bounciness` 0.4, and a `private hits: number` that starts at 0. Its
    `onReachedBottom` counts the hit and makes the ball paler with the
    attribute from research question 3, using `String(1 - this.hits * 0.3)` as
    the value. It returns `false` on the third hit.
12. Build the game loop below the classes:

    ```ts
    let balls: Ball[] = [];
    let lastTime = 0;

    const randomX = () => 50 + Math.random() * (STAGE_WIDTH - 100);

    const tick = (timestamp: number) => {
      if (lastTime === 0) {
        lastTime = timestamp;
      }
      const deltaSeconds = (timestamp - lastTime) / 1000;
      lastTime = timestamp;

      balls = balls.filter((ball) => ball.update(deltaSeconds));

      requestAnimationFrame(tick);
    };
    ```

    That one `filter` line updates every ball and keeps the survivors, because
    `update` returns exactly what `filter` wants to hear. A ball that dies has
    already taken its own circle out of the SVG in step 7.
13. Give each of the four ball buttons a `click` listener that pushes a new
    ball of its kind at `randomX()` into `balls`. Start the animation with one
    `requestAnimationFrame(tick);` at the end of the file. Expected result: every
    button drops a ball, the gummy ball changes color on each landing and comes
    to rest quickly, the steel ball bounces far longer, the super ball grows
    until it vanishes, and the fragile ball fades and is gone after three
    landings.
14. Wire the `#clear` button: call `remove()` on every ball in the array, then
    set `balls` to an empty array.
15. Bonus: add a fifth kind, a `PaintBall` that leaves a small circle behind on
    every landing. It needs the stage, so make the base class keep it in a
    `protected` field. Give it a sixth button in `index.html`, next to the
    other four, and wire it up the same way.
16. Run `npm run verify` and fix what it reports.

::: {.callout-note}
## What has to work

* The app starts with `npm start`, the console stays quiet, and
  `npm run verify` passes.
* `Ball` is `abstract`, and `bounciness` and `onReachedBottom` are abstract
  members that every kind fills in.
* No subclass repeats the physics from `update`.
* Balls never leave the box, and a ball that dies leaves neither a circle in
  the SVG nor an entry in the array.

A working `Clear` button and the fifth kind of ball from step 15 are what lift
this above passing.
:::
